opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it looks pretty different depending on the field, but there's a common thread.

In physics, where I come from, a lot of the work is a mix of deep conceptual thinking and a huge amount of grinding calculation: working through integrals, checking limits, searching the literature to see if someone already did this in 1987 under a different name. The grinding part is where AI tools are already really useful. If a model can carry out a long calculation, or at least check one, it frees you up to spend more time on the part that's actually creative: deciding which question is worth asking in the first place.

In fields like biology or chemistry, the picture is a bit different because there's so much data and the systems are so complex that there isn't always a clean theory to calculate from. There, models are useful as pattern-finders, for things like proposing candidate structures, suggesting experiments, or narrowing down a search space that would take a human lab years to explore. The bottleneck shifts toward the physical experiment, the wet lab, and AI helps you choose which experiments are worth running.

The common thread, I'd say, is that these tools change the economics of scientific labor. Things that used to be expensive in time and attention get cheap, and that changes what kinds of questions people are willing to pursue. A grad student who would have spent six months on a calculation might now spend a week, and then go ask a much more ambitious follow-up question.

Where I think it gets really interesting, and a little speculative, is the question of whether these systems go from being very good assistants to being genuine collaborators, actually generating new ideas and not just executing on ours. I don't think we're fully there yet, but the trajectory over the last few years has been steep enough that I take it seriously. And if that happens, it's not just faster science, it's potentially a different kind of science, where the limiting factor is less about how many smart people we can train and more about how well we can direct and verify what these systems produce.

So I'm optimistic, but I also think verification becomes the central skill. Knowing when the model is right, when it's subtly wrong, and how to check it is going to matter more than ever.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's going to look pretty different field by field, and that's actually the interesting part.

Where I'm coming from is theoretical physics, and in that world a lot of the day-to-day work is a mix of two things. There's the conceptual part, where you're trying to figure out what the right question even is, and then there's this enormous amount of technical labor: doing calculations, checking that an expansion is consistent, working through pages of algebra, writing code to simulate something. For the second category, these tools are already genuinely useful. They're like having a very fast, very well-read collaborator who's willing to grind through things with you and who has essentially read every paper. That changes the pace at which you can test ideas.

The first category, the "what should we even be asking" part, I think is where it's still early. But I don't think it's off the table. If you look at how physics has historically progressed, a lot of insight came from noticing analogies across subfields, and these models are unusually good at that kind of lateral connection because they've seen everything at once in a way no individual human has.

Now, if you move over to something like biology or chemistry, the bottleneck is different. There the constraint is often the experiment itself. You can have the best hypothesis in the world and still need months in the lab. So the role of AI there is more about prioritization: narrowing a huge space down to the handful of things worth actually testing, or designing experiments that are more informative per run. And then as labs get more automated, that loop between model and experiment starts to close, which I think is where some of the biggest gains will come from.

And in math, which is sort of the purest case, you're seeing something else again, which is these systems being used as a kind of reasoning partner that can actually check things rigorously. That's a very different flavor from the empirical sciences.

So the common thread, if there is one, is that the tools are compressing the part of research that is "known but laborious," and leaving more of the human time for the part that's genuinely uncertain. What I find exciting is that the ratio between those two is shifting, and I don't think we fully know yet what science looks like when the laborious part gets very cheap.

astra-6.text:
I think the role depends a lot on the field, but a useful way to think about AI is as a tool for shortening the loop between an idea and a test. That might mean helping someone analyze data, write code, explore a model, or identify a pattern they wouldn’t otherwise have noticed.

The crucial distinction is between generating a plausible hypothesis and establishing that it’s true. In science, you still need that second step—an experiment, a proof, or a prediction you can check against observations. AI can help with those steps, too, but a convincing explanation isn’t itself evidence.

So I’m excited about tools that give researchers more room to ask questions and test ideas. The details will look different across biology, physics, and the social sciences, but the question is the same: does this help us learn something we can actually verify?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role will vary by field, but a common thread is helping researchers move more quickly from a question to something they can test. That might mean exploring a large dataset, writing code, or finding connections across papers that would otherwise be difficult to spot.

The important distinction is between generating a plausible idea and establishing that it’s true. AI can help suggest hypotheses, but you still need experiments, careful analysis, and people who understand the subject to judge the results. The most useful tools will fit into that process and make their work easy to check.
